summary: Defines DHCP options that hand out the location of SLP Directory Agents and the scope settings used by the Service Location Protocol, so clients need not discover these separately.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a network, it hands you a sheet of useful info. This rule adds the spot to find the directory of services to that sheet.

questions: how to configure slp with dhcp
what is an slp directory agent
subtitle: Two DHCP options that tell SLP agents where their Directory Agents are and which scopes to use.

tldr.problem: SLP agents normally find Directory Agents by multicast or broadcast and use default scopes, which is hard to administer centrally and does not work where multicast routing is unavailable.
tldr.mechanism: Option 78 gives a list of Directory Agent addresses in order of preference, and option 79 gives a comma-delimited scope list, each with a Mandatory byte that controls how strongly it applies.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can configure SLP agents centrally through DHCP, with the caveat that DHCP information itself generally cannot be authenticated.

today: RFC 2610 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1999. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Configure SLP with DHCP
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (SLP), in versions 1 and 2, lets programs find network services. SLP agents need the addresses of Directory Agents (DAs) and a scope configuration. SLP has defaults for scopes, and DAs can be found by multicast or broadcast.

The RFC argues that in a larger deployment it is useful to configure SLP agents through DHCP. That centralizes administration and lets SLP be deployed in networks where multicast routing is not available. It defines two DHCP options for the job, which configure agents using both SLP version 2 and version 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every computer shouting to find the service directory, the network just tells it when it joins.

sections.title: The Two Options
sections.content:
The SLP Directory Agent option (code 78) tells User Agents and Service Agents where the Directory Agents are. The SLP Service Scope option (code 79) assigns scopes. The scope option takes precedence over both default and static scope configuration of SLP agents.

Both options carry a Mandatory byte right after the length. It decides how firmly the option binds the agent, as the next sections describe.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two notes on the sheet: one with the directory's address, one with the groups you belong to.

sections.title: SLP Directory Agent Option
sections.content:
Option 78 holds a list of IPv4 addresses of Directory Agents, in network byte order. They MUST be listed in order of preference if there is one. The Length counts one byte for Mandatory plus four for each address, so Length minus one MUST be divisible by 4 and the minimum Length is 5.

The Mandatory byte is 0 or 1. If it is 1, the agent MUST NOT use active or passive multicast discovery of Directory Agents. For backward compatibility with some deployed software, the byte MUST NOT have the high-order bit (0x80) set.

The listed DAs MUST be configured with a non-empty subset of the scope list that the receiving agent is configured with. How to use the option is defined in the SLPv2 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of directory addresses, best one first. A flag can say "do not go looking anywhere else."

sections.title: SLP Service Scope Option
sections.content:
Option 79 carries a comma-delimited scope list, encoded in UTF-8. Because UTF-8 characters can take more than one byte, Length may differ from the number of characters. Length includes one byte for Mandatory.

The Mandatory byte decides whether the DHCP scope list overrides the agent's static configuration. If it is 0, static configuration takes precedence. If it is 1, the scope list in the option MUST be used. This lets DHCP administrators enforce a policy of which scopes agents provide services in. The syntax and usage of the Scope List string are defined in the SLPv2 specification.

Empty scope list

A Length of 1, with no scope string at all, validly configures the User Agent to use "User Selectable Scopes." The agent then uses the combined scope lists of all known DAs, or, if none are known, uses SA discovery to learn the scopes on the network. The RFC warns this is tantamount to removing all centralized control of scopes, so every User Agent can see every service, which may not be desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: The note lists which groups you belong to. A flag decides whether this note beats what was already written on your computer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a malicious host can insert false information into DHCPOFFER packets sent to an SLP agent, the agent may be unable to get service or may be steered to the wrong services. The RFC lists many chances for denial of service: a service agent may rely on fraudulent Directory Agents, and DHCPOFFERs could tell clients not to use multicast or to use nonexistent Directory Agents.

The RFC says these difficulties come from a larger problem: in common DHCP deployments, securing or authenticating any information from a DHCP server (or client) is not possible.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sneaks a fake note onto the sheet, you might be sent to the wrong place. The network cannot yet tell real notes from fake ones.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: One for Mandatory plus four per address; minimum 5.

fields.name: Mandatory
fields.desc: 0 or 1; if 1, no multicast discovery of DAs.

fields.name: a1
fields.desc: First byte of the first DA address; more addresses may follow.
